records.our_prose: Small yellow spots appear on both surfaces of the leaves and enlarge into gray, roughly circular lesions about 1/4 to 3/4 inch across; as they multiply the tissue between them turns papery and often splits and cracks, and severe spotting blights the foliage. Plants weakened by calcium deficiency are especially susceptible. It is a rot of the dense, moist plant base rather than a leaf disease.

records.source_context: Management Symptoms and Signs Celery is susceptible to the pink rot fungus at all stages of plant growth, but the disease is most often observed on older plants when leaf canopies are well developed. Initial symptoms appear as brown lesions on the petioles that develop at or near the soil line or up in the plant canopy. Lesions rapidly expand into soft, watery, decayed areas.

records.our_prose: The young leaves and growing point in the center of the plant turn brown to black and die, while the outer stalks may still look healthy, so the damage is hidden until the plant is cut open. records.source_context: Water Good watering is essential to successful celery production. Celery needs at least 1 to 2 inches of water from rainfall or irrigation each week during the growing season. Always soak the soil thoroughly when watering because celery has a small, shallow root system.

records.our_prose: Air-temperature ceiling for celery quality. Extension sources put celery's optimum near 60 to 70°F (UC Master Gardeners of Santa Clara County give 60 to 65°F best, tolerating 45 to 75°F; Utah State gives an ideal of 55 to 65°F). Sustained air above roughly 75°F coarsens and bitters the stalks and, combined with drought, can trigger bolting, so the planting calendar in warm regions excludes the hottest months.

records.our_prose: Pale, winding, snakelike tunnels (mines) trace through the leaf tissue, and heavier infestations leave leaves blotched, blistered, and partly dried. The damage is the larvae feeding between the upper and lower leaf surfaces; pinprick stippling on the foliage marks where adult females punctured leaves to feed and lay eggs. Light mining is cosmetic, but a heavy attack reduces the plant's vigor and the eating quality of the leafy tops.

records.our_prose: In Florida, celery is a cool-season crop for fall, winter, and early spring: start seeds in late summer or early fall and plant out from fall into early winter for a winter-to-spring harvest (UF/IFAS lists roughly September to March). Summer is too hot and wet. The warm, damp weather brings leaf diseases, so use clean seed and keep the leaves dry.

records.our_prose: Summer gap is a HEAT exclusion, not a frost gap. Celery is a cool-season crop that grows best near 60 to 70°F and suffers above about 75°F: heat coarsens the stalks, turns them bitter, and combined with drought can trigger bolting, so the planting calendar in this region brackets the hottest months and grows celery in the cooler fall, winter, and spring windows. (UC Master Gardeners of Santa Clara County; Utah State University Extension; Texas A&M AgriLife Extension)

records.our_prose: This is the make-or-break stretch, while the stalks fill out. Celery needs more water, more steadily, than almost anything in the garden: at least 1 to 2 inches a week, more when hot, and never let it dry out even briefly. Drying out now makes the stalks tough, stringy, and bitter, and you cannot fix it later. Water at the base and keep the leaves and crowded plant base dry.

records.our_prose: This is the long, punishing window: as the stalks form and bulk up, celery is the thirstiest of the common vegetables and the least forgiving of any dry-down. Keep the soil evenly and constantly moist, at least 1 to 2 inches a week and more in heat, applied often at the base with the canopy and crown kept dry against blight and pink rot. Any interruption turns the petioles stringy, pithy, and bitter, and it does not reverse.
